extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, and news professionals interested in television news practice and production
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, conventions, and practical norms for producing and evaluating television news film and its narrative (camera placement, shot selection, pacing, framing, and organizational constraints that create an aura of 'facticity').

rubrics_metrics.name: Representational codes and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'representational' (applied to drawing, photographs, or news film) must refer to codes, conventions, and social schemata identified as representational by members of a specific culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that what appears as straightforward representation is culturally coded; examples include how Navajo filmmakers used sequences that match verbal storytelling conventions (e.g., walking sequences) and avoided close-ups. Evaluations should examine which cultural schemata are being invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim to actuality / facticity
rubrics_metrics.description: News film presents itself as 'actuality'—it claims to present facts rather than interpretations by refusing the appearance of manipulating time and space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the claim to facticity critically: acceptance of representational conventions as facticity makes reality vulnerable to manipulation. Identifying conventions as artful manipulations reframes filmed events as social accomplishments rather than raw facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of cinematic-fiction conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of news film claims neutrality and credibility by avoiding conventions associated with fiction (dramatic camera tricks, obvious stylization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fast or slow motion, dramatic angles, and other 'fictional' devices are typically condemned as 'distortion' and may lead to scolding or discarding of footage; assess whether such devices are used and whether they undermine the claimed neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricted use of slow/fast motion (permitted exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fast/slow motion is generally forbidden because it introduces interpretation (humor, tenderness), but there are exceptions (e.g., sports film for technical judgment; labeled slow motion used as 'analysis').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If slow/fast motion is used, it should be justifiable (sports analysis, clarifying sequence) and explicitly framed (e.g., labeled 'slow motion') to distinguish it from ordinary news film; otherwise it risks being discarded for impugning credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Head-on / eye-level camera placement for individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: For filming individuals (newsmakers, officials), camerawork should meet the event 'head on' with camera placement fixed to simulate the angle of a person of average height confronting another person eye to eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Head-on perspective is treated as nondistorting and thus factic; deviations are called 'distortion' and criticized. Evaluate whether subjects are filmed at this accepted perspective when neutrality is being claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of alternative (bird's-eye, worm's-eye) perspectives for participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative perspectives (high/low angles) are generally avoided when filming participants because they are labeled 'distortion' and can convert participants into objects or masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve such perspectives mainly for inanimate objects, landscapes, or when depicting crowds as masses; when used to film people, note the symbolic effect (objectification, depersonalization) and whether journalists justify the choice (e.g., safety, steadiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social distance/framing to convey neutrality (Hall distances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers use 'talking distance' framings (far personal, close social, far social) rather than 'touching' or 'public' distance to code social roles and convey noninvolvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess camera range: intimate or touching distances suggest involvement and drama (usually avoided); public distance depersonalizes and is 'unnewslike' for individuals. Correct framing maintains perceived impartiality while allowing emotional impact when desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard torso/head-and-shoulders shots for anchors/commentators
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchorpersons and commentators appear in standard torso shots emphasizing head and shoulders (and sometimes hands holding script) to project friendliness and neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistency in these shots across stories is itself a visual claim to neutrality; deviations (tight dramatic close-ups) signal drama or special status and are exceptions that must be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray reporters as detached from events (reporter framing and background treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters at scenes are framed somewhat farther from the camera (waist-up) with the event shown at a depersonalizing public distance in the background, signaling reporter detachment from the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing communicates the reporter's role as a nonparticipant; evaluate whether the reporter is presented as part of the event (involvement) or as detached (neutral describer). Exceptions when reporters become participants are treated as newsworthy anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic locations / iconic landmarks to claim 'at-scene' actuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing reporters against recognizable symbolic locations (e.g., White House portico, Big Ben) or showing city skylines signals that the reporter is actually at the scene and reinforces facticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers may re-shoot or reuse skyline footage to ensure recognizable context; inclusion of such exteriors is a standard device to situate stories and should be evaluated for authenticity vs staged reassurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event-coding through stereotypic visuals (stock symbols for story types)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events are encoded by the supposed essence of activity: strikes by picketers/locked gates, jungle wars by soldiers and helicopters, murders by blood on sidewalks, drug busts by piles of packets, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These quick visual signifiers allow immediate comprehension but compress complexity—assess whether such symbolic visuals oversimplify or misrepresent the underlying event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'average person' or 'symbol' interviewees to represent groups
rubrics_metrics.description: News film often presents ordinary individuals as symbols of a group (an 'average farmer', a 'typical small-town citizen') to stand for broader social conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate selection and framing of such interviewees (setting, camera range, emotional close-ups) to see how they are made to function as representatives rather than unique persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential framing to legitimate officials vs. depict challengers as masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Legitimated officials are filmed in neutral, head-on framings and associated with professional settings; challengers, demonstrators, or marginalized groups are often filmed from distances or angles that render them as depersonalized masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how camera choices contribute to legitimation: who is given the 'official' framing and who is objectified as part of a mass? Note the political implications of these visual role assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of jumpy/unstable camera work; preference for steady footage
rubrics_metrics.description: Jumpy film is dramatic and suggests tumult; news reporting aims to avoid such rendering of feeling by using steady shots (e.g., placing camera on rooftops or using helicopters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When unstable or high-angle footage is used, crews typically document and justify the choice to editors; unstated jumpy footage is usually criticized for undermining credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to a standard narrative form (avoid idiosyncratic/poetic treatments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Footage should conform to an accepted narrative form so it can be edited and integrated easily; poetic or highly idiosyncratic treatments are hard for viewers and editors to decode and are therefore discouraged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idiosyncratic footage risks reprimand, being 'worked over' or rejected by editors, and can harm a reporter's future assignments or relationships with technicians; evaluate footage for editability and narrative clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational workflow constraints shape footage (decodability by editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: News production is interdependent; crews must produce material that other staff (editors, cutters) can process quickly without extra decoding work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether material intentionally facilitates downstream work (standard shots, predictable pacing); deviations create organizational friction (backlogs, reprimands, loss of assignments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a limited lexicon of standard shots
rubrics_metrics.description: Television news employs a restricted repertoire of shots (a lexicon of ~50 standard shots and variations) so that film 'speaks' through codes intelligible across the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the shot choices adhere to the standard lexicon (promoting shared decoding) or deviate into novel forms (requiring special handling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and camera range as tools of role-prescription and neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Framings (distance, angle, setting) are used to prescribe social roles (reporters as detached professionals; anchors as friendly authorities; symbols as representatives) and to claim neutrality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging news film, attend to how camera range and framing enact role relationships and thereby construct the news organization's claims to impartiality and credibility.
